subject: Initial values have strong influence on posterior in community occupancy model

messages.author: c8888e6ccc8dadb4
messages.subject: Initial values have strong influence on posterior in community occupancy model
parts:
Dear group members,

I am fitting a community occupancy model (Dorazio-Royle model sensu Kéry & Royle 2016, p 690) to a wildlife camera dataset. The dimensions are
  • 120 sites
  • 2 occasions
  • 20 species detected and augmented by 50 (M = 70)
The detection/nondetection matrix contains 575 independent detections. 
Covariates for psi are
  • habitat (5 levels),
  • distance to closest human settlement,
  • distance to closed road,
  • relative abundance of humans, and
  • relative abundance of dogs.
Covariates for p are
  • body mass
  • distance to closest human settlement,
  • distance to closed road,
  • relative abundance of humans, and
  • relative abundance of dogs.
All continuous covariates are standardized. 

Whatever combination of initial values for metacommunity membership w and occupancy matrix Z I use, they strongly influence the posterior distribution of site occupancy and species richness: the outcome is either around 20 (the number of observed species) or around 70 (unconditional metacommunity size M). From literature I know that at least 29 species occur in the region.

 Now I wonder, what could be the reason for my model's behaviour and if there is any remedy? Is this model overfitting? Might there be lack of signal in the data?

As far as I can judge, the dimensions of the data and the model are comparable with many published examples I have seen; but, of course, you can proof me wrong.

Any comment on this is greatly appreciated!
Christoph

messages.author: c8888e6ccc8dadb4
messages.subject: Re: Initial values have strong influence on posterior in community occupancy model
parts:
Hello Diego,

thanks, I appreciate your help!

Yes, I was thinking the same and I build my model step by step:
  1. basic model: well behaved
  2. same as model 1 + with covariate body mass (on detection): well behaved
  3. same as model 2 + with covariates distance-to-village, distance-to-road, count-of-humans and count-of-dogs (on occupancy and detection): well behaved
  4. same as model 3 + with covariate habitat (five forest types): no mixing and convergence for richness measures
So, it's only model 4 (my "full" model) that behaves oddly, and this seems to have to do with the variable habitat or the way I included it in the model, for a fifth model (including habitat and body mass; excluding human pressure) behaves like model 4 (BUGS code of model 4 attached for inspection). Nevertheless a pairs plot shows no conspicuous patterns of any of the regression coefficients including habitat, but the derived richness values (Hill numbers) look bad and together with trace plots suggest that the MCMC do not explore their space at all: I have five chains and all of them oscillate more or less isolatedly around their value of N (see below: trace of hill number 2). From my naive understanding of Gibbs sampling, and if Hill numbers were not derived but integral part of the model, I would say the proposals must be more "venturous". As yet, JAGS is a blackbox to me and I don't know if I could fine-tune the MCMC and how do it. Any suggestions
are welcome!

Best wishes, Christoph

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: Initial values have strong influence on posterior in community occupancy model
parts:
Dear Christoph,

total non-mixing of the kind shown in your plots is sometimes due to an overparameterized model, i.e., when you try to squeeze more out of your data in terms of param estimates than what one can. So I was wondering whether perhaps you had in your model an intercept PLUS 5 parameters for the 5 habitat types. But that doesn't seem to be the case, so it can't be that. All the other covariates in the occupancy part of your model are continuous, right ? Nothing which represents two groups with two parameters (which then would lead to overparameterization) ?

I don't think there is a lot that one could tune in JAGS. For that you have to go to Nimble. This should be easy since the basic model-definition language is practically the same as the BUGS dialect in JAGS. Might be worth a try.

MCMC can be sensitive to parameterization of a model, i.e., how you specify a model in one of multiple equivalent ways. Sometimes miraculously one parameterization works much better than another. So that might be something that you could try. For instance, specify the occupancy part of the model as an intercept, plus 4 indicator variables for the differences of 4 habitat types relative to the baseline, plus the rest. Perhaps that leads to better mixing ?

Yet another idea: sometimes one may have what appears like total lack of mixing, but then suddenly the chains make a jump and converge. If you haven't already run your model for, say, a week (and you can do that), then I would try that as well.

All these are simply a blind chicken's try to find a grain. Somebody knowledgeable in MCMC might give more targeted advice.

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.author: 238422c6037ad1c9
messages.subject: Re: Initial values have strong influence on posterior in community occupancy model
parts:
Hello, 
After sen your code, I can see that there are a lot of parameters on it and as Marc wrote this can be an issue. 
Here is what I would do:
  • Make the precision parameters of the beta distribution the same, i mean:  tau.beta1.lpsi = ... =  tau.beta5.lpsi =  tau.lpsi, also do the same for  the tau.betan.lp. This is a strong assumption that may not be true, but it is just a try to reduce the over parametrisation, and if the outcome is good, then we have now better starting values. 
  • Try to use a different non informative prior, maybe make it a bit informative. If the model is strong enough and reaches convergence it will update to the best posterior distribution.
  • I think JAGS by default uses random walk sampler, maybe you can change this by doing block sampling, on your parameters \beta.lpsi and \beta.lp, you may have to be carefull with the correlation of the chains latter, but that is another issue. 
I hope this works, let me know.

-
Diego

messages.subject: Re: Initial values have strong influence on posterior in community occupancy model
parts: What initial values are you providing for w and Z? Any chance you are supplying initial values for latent states which aren't getting sampled by the model? If some latent states aren't getting sampled by the model, they will just remain with the initial values you provided, thereby giving very different output.

  • 20 species detected and augmented by 50 (M = 70)
The detection/nondetection matrix contains 575 independent detections. 
Covariates for psi are
  • habitat (5 levels),
  • distance to closest human settlement,
  • distance to closed road,
  • relative abundance of humans, and
  • relative abundance of dogs.
Covariates for p are
  • body mass
  • distance to closest human settlement,
  • distance to closed road,
  • relative abundance of humans, and
  • relative abundance of dogs.
All continuous covariates are standardized. 

Whatever combination of initial values for metacommunity membership w and occupancy matrix Z I use, they strongly influence the posterior distribution of site occupancy and species richness: the outcome is either around 20 (the number of observed species) or around 70 (unconditional metacommunity size M). From literature I know that at least 29 species occur in the region.

 Now I wonder, what could be the reason for my model's behaviour and if there is any remedy? Is this model overfitting? Might there be lack of signal in the data?

As far as I can judge, the dimensions of the data and the model are comparable with many published examples I have seen; but, of course, you can proof me wrong.

Any comment on this is greatly appreciated!
Christoph
